growth_story.headline: Nicaragua's income per person grew fastest in 2010–2017, fell in the 2018 crisis and now rests on remittances, yet stays below its 1977 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Nicaragua peaked in 1977 and is still 16.4 percent below that level, about where it first was in 1965, after war, debt and hyperinflation in the 1980s. From 1990 to 2009 it grew 1.3 percent a year: it kept falling until 1993, then recovered after a stabilization program in the early 1990s and, in the mid-2000s, debt relief, before dropping 4.7 percent in 2009. From 2010 to 2017 growth rose to 3.7 percent a year, a time when, the World Bank says, government and business worked closely, investment and exports were rising, and oil deals with Venezuela brought in large flows of money. The 2018 political crisis, then the pandemic and two hurricanes in 2020, cut income per person three years in a row, and the 2018–2025 era averages 1.0 percent a year. Since 2021 the recovery has been carried by money sent home by emigrants and by high prices for gold, coffee and beef, with income per person up 3.6 percent in 2025. Over the last decade growth averaged 1.4 percent a year, against 2.7 in the decade before.

threads.title: War, hyperinflation and debt relief
threads.text: The 1980s left Nicaragua deep in debt, with hyperinflation and a weak economy after years of conflict. A stabilization program in the early 1990s brought inflation down, and debt relief in the mid-2000s freed money for social and infrastructure spending, helping the slow recovery of the 1990–2009 era.

threads.text: The faster growth of 2010–2017 came with a close working relationship between the government and private firms, and with large flows from oil cooperation with Venezuela. Those flows had nearly dried up by 2018 as Venezuela's own economy worsened.

threads.title: The 2018 crisis and 2020 shocks
threads.text: Protests over pension reforms in April 2018 turned into a political crisis that drove money out of banks and the country. The pandemic and two hurricanes followed in 2020, so income per person fell in 2018, 2019 and 2020 before rebounding 9.1 percent in 2021.

threads.text: Emigration rose sharply from mid-2021, and most of the money emigrants send home comes from the United States. Remittances now support household spending, and exports are no longer the main driver of growth, which leaves the economy exposed to changes in U.S. immigration policy.

threads.title: Sanctions, seizures and fading investment
threads.text: Since 2018 the U.S., the EU, the UK and Canada have placed targeted sanctions on some officials and state bodies. Since 2022 the state has taken over more property from closed non-profit groups, citizens stripped of their nationality and some companies, and net foreign investment has been falling as a share of the economy.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 3.6 percent in 2025, helped by high world prices for gold, coffee and beef and by rising remittances. Exporters began absorbing higher tariffs from April 2025, and more migrants came home while fewer left for the United States. The World Bank's October 2026 outlook expects growth to slow as remittances and foreign investment fall with shifts in U.S. policy.

growth_story.tension: The IMF wrote that real GDP had passed its pre-crisis level by the end of 2021, but income per person, which also counts a growing population, did not pass its 2017 level until 2023. The IMF also says the economy weathered the shocks since 2018 well, yet the 2018–2025 era averages 1.0 percent a year, the slowest of the three eras since 1990.
